articles.summary: Liontown Resources (ASX:LTR), Core Lithium (ASX:CXO) and Kantra Copper (ASX:KAN): What Lies Ahead for Lithium and Copper?  Kalkine
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Lithium market conditions remain sensitive to battery demand, production levels and changes in global supply.
- Liontown Resources (ASX:LTR) and Core Lithium (ASX:CXO) have different operational priorities within Australia's lithium sector.
- Wildcat Resources (ASX:WC8) and PMET Resources (ASX:PMT) continue progressing their respective lithium development projects.
- Copper companies remain exposed to infrastructure investment, electrification and changing global supply conditions.
Australia's lithium industry continues to navigate fluctuations in commodity demand, production costs and global supply conditions. As of 12 October 2026, developments across battery materials markets remain relevant to producers and project developers.
Lithium demand is closely connected to electric vehicle manufacturing and battery energy storage systems. Both applications require reliable supplies of battery materials, although purchasing patterns can vary depending on manufacturing schedules, inventories and government policies.
Seasonal changes in Chinese industrial activity can influence short-term trading conditions. However, attributing lithium price movements entirely to seasonal factors would overlook broader influences such as inventories, production levels and battery manufacturing demand.
Australian companies including Liontown Resources (ASX:LTR), PLS Group (ASX:PLS), Mineral Resources (ASX:MIN), IGO (ASX:IGO) and Elevra Lithium (ASX:ELV) operate across different parts of the lithium supply chain.
Their operational performance is influenced by commodity prices, production efficiency, processing costs and individual project requirements.
Liontown and Core Lithium Have Distinct Operational Priorities
Liontown Resources (ASX:LTR) operates the Kathleen Valley lithium project in Western Australia, a significant hard-rock lithium development.
The company's operational priorities include production performance, processing efficiency and the management of its mine development activities. Sustained operational improvements remain important as Liontown works within a changing lithium market.
Core Lithium (ASX:CXO), meanwhile, has focused on repositioning its Finniss Lithium Project in the Northern Territory.
The company previously completed a restart study examining a revised underground mining approach, processing improvements and potential operating cost reductions.
Unlike an established operating mine, a project preparing for a restart faces additional requirements involving financing, operational readiness, development expenditure and market conditions.
Consequently, Liontown Resources (ASX:LTR) and Core Lithium (ASX:CXO) have different operational considerations despite their exposure to the same underlying commodity.
Wildcat Resources and PMET Progress Lithium Development
Wildcat Resources (ASX:WC8) is progressing its Tabba Tabba lithium project in Western Australia's Pilbara region.
The company has undertaken exploration, resource definition and technical investigations to support the project's development pathway.
Wildcat Resources (ASX:WC8) has also worked towards a definitive feasibility study, with environmental approvals and project engineering forming important components of its development process.
PMET Resources (ASX:PMT) is advancing the Shaakichiuwaanaan project in Quebec, Canada.
Its development activities include technical studies, mineral resource evaluation and assessments of lithium and associated critical minerals.
The company has also outlined financing initiatives intended to support further exploration and feasibility work.
For both Wildcat Resources (ASX:WC8) and PMET Resources (ASX:PMT), progress towards production depends on the completion of technical studies, regulatory approvals, financing and development decisions.
Copper Demand Remains Linked to Infrastructure Development
Copper occupies an important position in electricity transmission, industrial manufacturing, renewable energy infrastructure and data centre construction.
Demand associated with electrification and expanding electricity networks provides a structural consideration for the copper industry.
However, future market conditions will also depend on mine production, project development timelines, processing capacity and global economic activity.
Australian-listed copper businesses include KGL Resources (ASX:KGL), Prospect Resources (ASX:PSC), FireFly Metals (ASX:FFM) and AIC Mines (ASX:A1M).
These companies have differing operating profiles, ranging from established mining activities to projects undergoing exploration and development assessments.
FireFly Metals (ASX:FFM), for example, is progressing its Green Bay copper-gold project in Canada, where metallurgical investigations and engineering studies are intended to inform future development decisions.
Project economics across the copper sector remain dependent on recoveries, capital requirements, operating costs and commodity prices.
Kantra Copper Expands Its Operational and Development Focus
Kantra Copper (ASX:KAN), formerly Hillgrove Resources, operates the Kanmantoo underground copper mine in South Australia.
The company's published 2026 production guidance was 12,750–14,000 tonnes of copper, supported by underground development and mining activities at Kanmantoo.
Kantra Copper (ASX:KAN) has also entered a farm-in agreement with Havilah Resources (ASX:HAV) relating to the Mutooroo copper project near Broken Hill.
Under the arrangement, Kantra can earn an 80% interest in Mutooroo, subject to specified conditions. The proposed development pathway includes assessing the potential to process Mutooroo material using existing Kanmantoo infrastructure.
The arrangement provides an additional development opportunity, although further metallurgical, engineering and economic assessments are required before investment decisions.
Key Insights
As of 12 October 2026, Australian lithium and copper companies face different operational and development priorities.
Liontown Resources (ASX:LTR), Core Lithium (ASX:CXO), Wildcat Resources (ASX:WC8) and PMET Resources (ASX:PMT) remain exposed to lithium market conditions, while Kantra Copper (ASX:KAN) is focused on copper production and evaluating additional development opportunities.
Future developments will depend on commodity demand, project execution, regulatory approvals and capital availability.

articles.title: Critical Minerals: 5 Smart Bets in a Powerful New Race - Global Brands Magazine
articles.summary: Critical Minerals: 5 Smart Bets in a Powerful New Race  Global Brands Magazine
articles.full_text:
Every electric car, wind turbine, data centre and smartphone rests on a short list of raw materials that most people never think about. Critical minerals, the group that includes lithium, copper, cobalt, nickel, graphite and the rare earths, have quietly become some of the most strategically important commodities on the planet. In 2026 the race to secure them has moved from mining conferences into corporate boardrooms.
The reason is demand. According to the International Energy Agency, lithium demand is projected to rise roughly 353% between 2024 and 2040, while graphite demand could climb about 131%. Global battery demand alone grew more than 35% in 2025, passing 1.5 terawatt-hours, with grid-scale storage joining electric vehicles as a major pull. These are not niche materials any more. They are the building blocks of the electrified economy.
Why critical minerals matter now
The shift is being driven by three overlapping trends. Electric vehicles need large batteries, and batteries need lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite. Electricity grids are expanding and modernising, which takes enormous quantities of copper. And the motors, magnets and electronics inside everything from wind turbines to robots depend on rare earth elements. Add fast-growing demand for computing power, and the pressure on supply only builds.
For companies, that turns raw materials into a competitive issue. A carmaker without secure battery materials cannot promise buyers a steady supply. An electronics firm exposed to a single source of rare earths carries a risk it may not fully understand. What used to be a purchasing detail is now a question of corporate resilience.
A concentrated supply chain
The awkward truth about critical minerals is that supply is heavily concentrated, especially in the refining stage where raw ore becomes usable material. The IEA notes that for copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths, the combined market share of the top three refining nations rose to about 86% in 2024, up from around 82% in 2020. Battery recycling capacity is even more concentrated, with one country accounting for roughly 90% of material recovery capacity.
| Mineral | Projected demand growth (2024-2040) | 
|---|---|
| Lithium | ~+353% | 
| Graphite | ~+131% | 
| Copper, nickel, rare earths | Strong, steady growth | 
| Global battery demand (2025) | +35% year on year, past 1.5 TWh | 
Concentration is not a moral judgement, it is a business risk. When most of the world’s refining or recycling sits in a few places, a single disruption, whether weather, technical or logistical, can ripple through every industry that depends on the output. That is why diversification has become a strategic priority for so many companies at once.
The companies that treat critical minerals as an afterthought today are the ones most likely to be caught short tomorrow.
The recycling opportunity
One of the most promising responses is recycling. Today, average recycling rates across key energy minerals sit at roughly 10%, but the IEA expects that to climb towards 20% by 2040 under current policies, with cobalt and copper further ahead. Recovering minerals from used batteries and scrap could become a meaningful second source of supply, and a business in its own right, though it needs sustained investment in collection and processing to reach its potential.
The scale of investment required is large. Diversifying magnet rare earth supply chains alone would take around $60 billion over the next decade, by IEA estimates. That is capital looking for a return, which is exactly why miners, manufacturers and investors are circling the sector.
Recycling has a second benefit beyond supply. Recovering critical minerals from old devices and batteries uses far less energy and water than digging fresh ore, which appeals to companies under pressure to shrink their environmental footprint. It also keeps valuable material inside the economies that already own it, rather than shipping it out as waste and buying it back later as finished product. For brands that want a supply story they can stand behind, a credible recycling loop is becoming a genuine advantage.
Copper, the quiet giant
Lithium and rare earths grab the headlines, but copper may be the most important critical mineral of all, because almost nothing electrifies without it. Every electric car, charging point, solar farm, wind turbine and data centre needs large amounts of copper wiring, and demand keeps climbing as grids expand to carry more power. Unlike some exotic materials, copper is mined and used at massive scale, which makes even small imbalances between supply and demand ripple widely through prices.
New copper mines take a long time to bring online, often a decade or more from discovery to production. That lag is exactly why analysts worry about a squeeze later this decade, as demand from electrification and computing runs ahead of new supply. For companies planning long-lived investments, from carmakers to utilities, copper is no longer something to take for granted. It is a strategic input to be secured well in advance.
The same pattern shows up across the group. Building a new mine, refinery or recycling plant is slow and capital-intensive, while demand can shift quickly. That mismatch between fast demand and slow supply is the core tension in critical minerals, and it is why the topic has jumped up the corporate agenda rather than staying in the commodities pages.
How companies are securing critical minerals
The corporate playbook is taking shape. Manufacturers are signing long-term offtake deals directly with miners, sometimes years before a mine opens, to lock in supply. Some are investing in mining and refining projects themselves rather than relying on the open market. Others are building recycling operations to create a domestic loop. And a wave of consolidation is under way, as shown by high-profile talks such as those we covered between Glencore and Rio Tinto.
Investment is following the demand. Mining and refining projects that struggled to raise money a few years ago are attracting fresh capital, and specialist funds have sprung up to back critical minerals ventures from exploration through to recycling. Governments and large manufacturers are co-investing too, sharing the risk of building supply that may take years to come good. For patient investors, the appeal is a rare combination of structural demand growth and genuine scarcity, though the sector carries real risks around cost overruns, permitting and price swings.
The corporate lesson is to map exposure before it becomes a crisis. That means knowing which critical minerals sit inside your products, where they are refined, and what would happen if a single source went offline. Firms that can answer those questions calmly are in a far stronger position than those discovering the answer during a shortage. Increasingly, that mapping is being done at board level, alongside the traditional risks of currency, cyber and demand.
The through-line connects to stories GBM has followed elsewhere, from the race to commercialise solid-state batteries to the business of carbon capture and the wider return of hardware. All of them depend, in the end, on getting enough of the right materials at a price that works. Critical minerals have become the quiet foundation of the next industrial era, and the companies treating them as a strategic priority are the ones building on solid ground. For more, see our reports and insights coverage.

Highlights
- Russia holds 28.4 million tonnes of rare-earth reserves across 18 deposits but extracts only ~2,200 tonnes annually, with commercial output limited to the Lovozero loparite deposit.
- Rosatom is consolidating the Lovozero mine with the Solikamsk Magnesium Plant, targeting a 2,500-tonne-per-year separated rare-earth oxide facility by 2028.
- Russia already dominates global palladium supply at 41% and holds strategic positions in vanadium, nickel, and cobalt, making it systemically important beyond rare earths.
- India-Russia cooperation is advancing through agreements between GIREDMET and India's TEXMiN and Nexon Geochem covering REE processing, NdFeB magnets, and pilot validation.
- Investors are warned not to conflate geological reserves with market-ready supply—Russia's critical mineral future will be decided in separation plants, not on geological maps.

articles.title: EU’s new strategic projects for critical raw materials include three for lithium extraction - Balkan Green Energy News
articles.summary: EU’s new strategic projects for critical raw materials include three for lithium extraction  Balkan Green Energy News
articles.full_text:
The European Commission has selected 46 more strategic projects for critical raw materials across 16 member states. Three are for lithium extraction, of which one for a hard rock mine, and two for obtaining the alkali metal from geothermal waters. Together with the ones approved previously, 13 strategic projects for battery-grade lithium involve extraction, and another 13 are just for processing and-or recycling.
The EU has so far endorsed 106 strategic projects for critical raw materials to bolster its supply and become less dependent on any single supplier. The second round consists of 46 selected proposals from 16 member states, out of this year’s 102 applications.
Per the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), extraction must cover at least 10% of consumption in 2030, alongside a 40% domestic share in processing and 25% from recycling.
Eight projects in the new group are for extraction only, 11 for processing, and 19 for recycling. Eight are integrated projects: three combine extraction and processing, and five are for both processing and recycling. Altogether they cover 15 of the 17 strategic raw materials.
The strategic projects endorsed so far are set to meet the EU’s benchmarks for lithium extraction
The new strategic projects are intended to strengthen European value chains. They include seven for battery-grade lithium, 12 for nickel, 10 for cobalt, five for manganese and four for graphite, all of which support the EU battery value chain. The two for magnesium and three for tungsten would contribute to defence and aerospace, while the four projects for rare earth elements would support the permanent magnet value chain, the European Commission said.
Together with last year’s 47 strategic projects in the EU and the 13 in third countries, they could fully meet the extraction benchmarks for lithium, nickel, rare earth elements, magnesium and tungsten, and the processing benchmarks for lithium and rare earth elements. They could also cover 89% of the processing benchmark for cobalt and 57% and 51% for tungsten and magnesium, respectively, while fully meeting the recycling benchmarks for lithium, cobalt and rare earth elements, the announcement reads.
Lithium is essential for battery energy storage systems (BESS) including batteries for electric vehicles.
Nine lithium mines on EU’s list of strategic projects
Just one new endeavor, Zinnwald Lithium Project in Germany, involves lithium excavation. In comparison, seven mining proposals for lithium were approved in 2025, alongside Rio Tinto’s project Jadar, which is in the group outside of the EU – and dormant.
Separately, there are now four strategic projects in total for extracting the alkali metal from geothermal waters of which two are new. The emerging technology has a neglectable environmental impact compared to mining. Thirteen selected proposals are just for lithium processing and-or recycling.
The production of lithium and geothermal heat can bolster each other’s cost-effectiveness
AMG Critical Materials, based in Amsterdam, bought the remaining 71% of the Zinnwald Lithium firm last year. The site for the hard rock mine is near Altenberg in Saxony, along the Czech-German border. It would include a processing facility.
Lithium de France, a subsdiary of Arverne, is working on a geothermal lithium extraction and processing system in northern Alsace. The project aspires to reach battery-quality lithium output of 27,000 tons per year, together with 2 TWh of heat.
The combination of geothermal energy and lithium can boost the cost-effectiveness of both otherwise expensive technologies.
Similarly, Neptune Energy Innovations would produce and process the material from deep thermal waters under the strategic project called ALE – Altmark Lithium Extraction.
Romania to host battery recycling facility
One new battery recycling project is in Germany and another one in the Netherlands. One just for lithium processing and recycling is in Germany.
As for the region that Balkan Green Energy News tracks, a strategic project in Romania called Eco Life Style was selected for battery recycling, to obtain cobalt, lithium, manganese, graphite and nickel. The site is in Răcari, just northwest of Bucharest.
In Greece, a copper extraction project was endorsed, and one each for the recycling of copper and aluminum. Bulgaria now hosts one, for copper processing.
Progress of strategic projects from first list
As for the group selected last year, 25 strategic projects have completed their environmental impact assessments and 17 have obtained construction permits.
Since the launch of the RESourceEU initiative, the bloc has mobilised more than EUR 2 billion in financial support through the Innovation Fund, state aid and the European Investment Bank, the update reads.
Several projects have made significant progress towards securing offtake agreements, the European Commission said. In addition, the Raw Materials Mechanism, established to aggregate demand and supply and identify potential offtakers, has generated more than 30 matches for 10 materials.
Promoters of strategic projects need to secure financing, complete the necessary permitting procedures, and comply with all applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
A call for strategic project applications is due before the end of 2026.

Stanislav Kondrashov on Europe's critical minerals future
Stanislav Kondrashov examines the latest developments in Europe's critical raw materials strategy, focusing on the growing importance of mineral processing, recycling infrastructure, and supply chain diversification for the continent's industrial future.
Europe's approach to critical raw materials is entering a new phase, characterized by an increasing emphasis on industrial integration and the development of strategic capabilities. As reported by Reuters, the European Commission has selected 46 additional strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act, reinforcing the European Union's efforts to improve access to resources essential for modern industry.
Distributed across 16 EU member states, these projects represent an estimated investment requirement of €21.1 billion. They involve a broad range of strategically important materials, including lithium, copper, nickel, graphite, and rare earth elements.
The most important development is the growing recognition that mineral security depends not only on resource availability, but also on the industrial infrastructure required to process, refine, and recycle these materials.
The latest selection reflects a more comprehensive vision of European mineral security, connecting resource development with manufacturing capabilities and technological competitiveness.
How Is Europe's Critical Raw Materials Strategy Evolving?
Europe's critical raw materials strategy is evolving toward a more integrated industrial model that combines domestic production capabilities, advanced processing infrastructure, recycling, and international supply diversification. The latest selection of strategic projects demonstrates the European Union's intention to address vulnerabilities across multiple stages of mineral supply chains.
Several figures illustrate the scope of this development:
- 46 new strategic projects selected under the Critical Raw Materials Act.
- 16 EU member states involved in the latest selection.
- €21.1 billion in estimated investment requirements.
- 15 of the 17 strategic raw materials covered by the newly selected initiatives.
- 106 strategic projects in the broader framework, including initiatives outside the European Union.
The first European selection, announced in March 2025, included 47 projects. The latest round further expands the framework, supporting the development of a more diversified and interconnected industrial ecosystem.
"Europe's latest initiatives highlight an important transformation in the way mineral security is understood. The strategic objective is no longer limited to identifying new resources, but increasingly involves creating the industrial conditions necessary to transform those resources into valuable materials for European manufacturers," says Stanislav Kondrashov.
This evolution is particularly relevant in sectors where access to raw materials depends on complex international supply networks and specialized processing technologies.
Why Are Mineral Processing and Recycling Becoming Strategic Priorities?
Mineral processing and recycling are becoming central priorities because they can reduce Europe's dependence on external facilities and strengthen the availability of industrial materials. Of the 46 newly selected projects, only eight are classified as exclusively extractive, while the others involve processing, recycling, or combinations of different activities.
This distribution reflects the importance of developing capabilities throughout the mineral value chain.
Extracting a mineral does not automatically make it suitable for industrial applications. Many resources require specialized treatment, chemical processing, separation, or refining before they can be incorporated into finished products.
Lithium, for example, must undergo specific processing stages before becoming suitable for many battery technologies. Rare earth elements require sophisticated separation procedures to obtain materials used in permanent magnets and other advanced applications.
Without adequate processing infrastructure, European industries may remain dependent on foreign facilities even when mineral resources are available domestically.
Recycling offers another opportunity to strengthen supply security. Recovering minerals from batteries, electronic equipment, and industrial components can provide secondary sources of valuable materials while complementing primary resource production.
However, the effectiveness of recycling depends on collection systems, technological development, and the availability of recoverable materials.
Lithium, Nickel, and Graphite: Supporting Europe's Battery Supply Chains
The growing strategic importance of Europe's battery industry is reflected in the presence of several battery-related minerals among the resources addressed by the latest projects.
These materials support different technological and industrial applications:
- Lithium: Widely used in rechargeable battery technologies.
- Nickel: Important for certain high-energy-density battery chemistries.
- Graphite: A principal material used in lithium-ion battery anodes.
- Cobalt: Relevant to selected battery cathode technologies.
- Manganese: Used in battery manufacturing and metallurgical applications.
- Copper: Essential for electrical systems, energy infrastructure, and industrial electrification.
The development of European processing capacity for these resources could support a more integrated battery manufacturing ecosystem.
"Battery supply chains demonstrate how closely mineral resources and advanced manufacturing are connected. Developing reliable access to lithium, nickel, and graphite is important, but Europe must also consider the technological capabilities required to transform these materials into products suitable for industrial use," explains Stanislav Kondrashov.
Rare Earths and Industrial Applications Beyond Renewable Energy
Critical minerals are essential to a wide range of industries beyond renewable energy and electric mobility.
Rare earth elements are used in permanent magnets, electronics, and specialized equipment. Their processing often requires advanced technologies, making separation and refining capabilities particularly important.
Other strategic materials, including magnesium and tungsten, contribute to aerospace, defense, metallurgy, and high-performance manufacturing.
These applications demonstrate that critical raw materials support a broad industrial ecosystem.
Europe's mineral strategy is therefore closely connected to technological development, manufacturing resilience, and the long-term competitiveness of several strategic sectors.
Which European Projects Illustrate This Industrial Transformation?
Several initiatives included in the latest selection demonstrate how European countries are contributing to the development of diversified mineral supply chains.
In Germany, a Lithium project illustrates the potential importance of domestic lithium resources for European battery-related industries.
Greece's project, associated with copper and gold, represents another example of mineral resource development within the European strategic framework.
In France, initiatives involving rare earth separation highlight the importance of specialized processing technologies.
These projects reflect different aspects of the European approach, from resource development to advanced industrial transformation.
Their geographical distribution also demonstrates the potential contribution of different European regions, each with distinct geological characteristics and technological capabilities.
Does Strategic Designation Guarantee Financing and Development?
Strategic designation under the Critical Raw Materials Act does not guarantee financing or the completion of individual projects. The estimated €21.1 billion associated with the latest selection represents required investment, rather than funding already allocated by European institutions.
Nevertheless, strategic recognition can provide advantages through administrative coordination, permitting procedures, and improved access to potential financing opportunities.
Projects must still address technical, environmental, financial, and commercial requirements before becoming operational.
"The designation of strategic projects is an important step, but the real measure of progress will be their implementation. Investment mobilization, technological expertise, and effective coordination between institutions and industry will be essential to translate Europe's mineral ambitions into functioning industrial capacity," concludes Stanislav Kondrashov.
What Could These Initiatives Mean for Europe's Long-Term Mineral Security?
The new projects could contribute to Europe's mineral security by strengthening domestic industrial capabilities and reducing excessive concentration across international supply chains.
The broader European strategy combines several complementary priorities:
- Expanding domestic resource development where economically and technically feasible.
- Strengthening mineral processing and refining infrastructure.
- Increasing recycling capabilities and secondary material recovery.
- Diversifying supply relationships through international partnerships.
- Supporting industrial sectors dependent on strategically important minerals.
This approach does not necessarily imply complete European self-sufficiency.
Instead, it reflects an effort to establish more reliable and diversified sources of supply while developing the industrial capabilities needed to support advanced manufacturing.

TELF AG on Europe's critical mineral strategy
Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG, examines the strategic implications of Europe's latest critical raw materials initiatives, highlighting the growing importance of processing capacity, recycling infrastructure, and diversified mineral supply chains.
The European Union is entering a new phase in its efforts to strengthen the availability of critical raw materials. As recently reported by Reuters, the European Commission has selected 46 additional strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act, expanding a European industrial initiative designed to reduce supply vulnerabilities and reinforce the continent's position in strategically important mineral value chains.
The newly selected projects, distributed across 16 EU member states, represent an estimated investment requirement of €21.1 billion. Their significance extends beyond the extraction of mineral resources, encompassing processing, recycling, and the integration of different industrial activities.
The central development is Europe's increasing emphasis on building complete mineral supply chains rather than concentrating exclusively on domestic mining operations.
This approach reflects the recognition that access to mineral deposits alone cannot guarantee industrial autonomy. The ability to transform raw materials into products suitable for manufacturing is equally important, particularly in sectors such as batteries, renewable energy, aerospace, and defense.
How Is Europe Expanding Its Critical Raw Materials Strategy?
The European Union is expanding its critical minerals strategy by identifying industrial projects capable of supporting different stages of the raw materials supply chain. The latest selection of 46 initiatives follows an earlier round announced in March 2025, reinforcing a broader effort to develop domestic capabilities and diversify international sourcing.
The principal figures illustrate the scale of this initiative:
- 46 new strategic projects selected in the latest European round.
- 16 EU member states involved in the newly designated initiatives.
- €21.1 billion in estimated investment requirements.
- 15 of the 17 strategic raw materials covered by the new projects.
- 106 strategic projects in total, including initiatives located outside the European Union.
These figures suggest that the European approach is becoming increasingly comprehensive, with industrial planning extending from mineral extraction to the technological processes required to make those resources commercially usable.
"The most significant aspect of this new selection is the growing attention devoted to the entire mineral value chain. Europe appears increasingly aware that securing access to raw materials is only the first step: the real industrial challenge is developing the capabilities needed to process, refine, and integrate those resources into manufacturing systems," says Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.
The distinction is particularly important for minerals whose supply chains are geographically concentrated. Even when a country possesses substantial geological resources, the absence of suitable processing infrastructure can leave its manufacturers dependent on facilities located elsewhere.
Why Are Processing and Recycling Becoming Central to Europe's Mineral Supply Chains?
Processing and recycling are becoming increasingly important because they can help Europe reduce its reliance on external industrial infrastructure. The latest project selection demonstrates this evolution: only eight of the 46 initiatives are classified as exclusively extractive, while the others involve processing, recycling, or combinations of different activities.
This distribution reveals an important feature of the European strategy.
For many critical minerals, extraction represents only the beginning of a complex industrial sequence. Lithium, for example, must undergo several processing stages before it can become suitable for battery manufacturing. Rare earth elements require specialized separation and refining technologies before they can be incorporated into advanced industrial components.
Europe's challenge is therefore not simply to obtain more minerals, but to increase its ability to transform them into materials that European industries can use.
Recycling represents another essential dimension of this approach. Recovering valuable resources from batteries, industrial equipment, and other products can create secondary sources of supply while reducing the amount of material that must be obtained through new mining operations.
However, recycling cannot immediately replace primary extraction. Its contribution depends on the availability of recyclable materials, collection systems, recovery technologies, and economically viable industrial processes.
The development of integrated supply chains could therefore help Europe combine several complementary sources of mineral availability.
Lithium, Nickel, and Copper: The Industrial Importance of Battery Materials
The prominence of lithium, nickel, copper, cobalt, and manganese among the resources addressed by the projects highlights the strategic importance of Europe's battery industry.
These materials contribute to different aspects of electrification and energy infrastructure:
- Lithium: A fundamental component of many rechargeable battery technologies.
- Nickel: Used in several high-energy-density battery chemistries.
- Cobalt: Important in certain battery cathode formulations.
- Manganese: Used in various battery technologies and industrial applications.
- Copper: Essential for electrical conductivity, power networks, and electrification systems.
- Graphite: Widely used in lithium-ion battery anodes.
Their industrial relevance extends beyond electric vehicles. Energy storage systems, electrical infrastructure, and numerous advanced manufacturing processes also depend on reliable access to these resources.
"The European battery industry provides a particularly clear example of how mineral availability and industrial competitiveness are connected. Developing extraction projects can strengthen the supply base, but processing capacity and the production of battery-grade materials are equally important for creating a resilient manufacturing ecosystem," explains Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.
Rare Earths and Strategic Minerals Beyond the Energy Transition
Although the energy transition occupies a prominent position in discussions about critical raw materials, Europe's mineral requirements extend into several other industrial sectors.
Rare earth elements are used in permanent magnets, electronic equipment, and advanced technologies. Certain applications are particularly relevant to electric motors, wind turbines, and specialized industrial machinery.
Other materials, including magnesium and tungsten, play important roles in aerospace, defense, metallurgy, and high-performance manufacturing.
The strategic significance of these resources therefore cannot be evaluated exclusively through their contribution to renewable energy or electric mobility.
Critical raw materials are increasingly relevant to the broader technological and industrial capabilities of the European economy.
Which European Projects Illustrate This New Industrial Direction?
Several initiatives included in the latest selection demonstrate the diversity of Europe's approach to mineral supply chains.
In Germany, a lithium-related project reflects the importance of developing domestic resources capable of supporting the European battery industry.
In Greece, the Skouries project, associated with copper and gold, illustrates the continuing relevance of mining activities within the broader strategy.
Sweden's copper project highlights the potential contribution of regions with established mining traditions, while a French initiative focused on rare earth separation emphasizes the importance of advanced processing infrastructure.
These examples demonstrate that Europe's strategy is not based on a single industrial model.
Instead, different countries and regions can contribute through their particular geological resources, technological capabilities, and existing industrial infrastructure.
Some projects may increase primary mineral production, while others could strengthen refining capacity or improve the recovery of materials already circulating within the European economy.
Does Strategic Project Status Guarantee Funding and Implementation?
Strategic designation under the Critical Raw Materials Act does not automatically guarantee financial support or the successful completion of a project. The estimated €21.1 billion associated with the latest selection represents investment requirements, not money already allocated by the European Commission.
This distinction is essential for understanding the practical significance of the announcement.
Strategic status can provide advantages through more coordinated administrative procedures, permitting frameworks, and support in accessing potential financing opportunities.
However, individual projects must still address commercial, technical, financial, and environmental considerations.
The transition from strategic designation to operational capacity therefore remains a crucial challenge.
"The selection of strategic projects represents an important institutional signal, but the decisive results will emerge during implementation. Financing, technical execution, permitting procedures, and industrial coordination will determine how effectively these initiatives contribute to Europe's long-term mineral security," concludes Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.

The latest European selection points toward a more integrated understanding of mineral security, in which extraction, processing, recycling, and international partnerships operate as interconnected components of industrial policy.

The government is expected to announce its critical minerals stockpiling policy within a month to strengthen supply security for strategic sectors, including defence, advanced electronics and aerospace. Mines Secretary Keshav Chandra announced the government’s efforts to secure essential mineral resources for domestic industries. “We are on the verge of finalising the policy on stockpiling of critical minerals which will be announced in about a month’s time,” Chandra informed during the India Mines and Minerals Conclave 2026, organised by industry body Assocham. The proposed policy aims to ensure a reliable supply of critical minerals required for manufacturing, technological development and strategic applications.
Government Plans Four Critical Minerals Processing Parks
Alongside the stockpiling policy, the government plans to establish four dedicated critical minerals processing parks in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. According to the mines secretary, these parks will accelerate domestic mineral processing and value addition, particularly for materials used in battery manufacturing. The initiative is expected to strengthen India’s mineral processing ecosystem and reduce reliance on external supply chains.
More Than 30 Critical Minerals Identified
The government has identified more than 30 minerals as critical, considering the requirements of key sectors such as defence, agriculture, energy, pharmaceuticals and telecommunications. These minerals play an important role in industrial production, advanced technologies and national infrastructure. Securing their availability is therefore essential to support economic growth and strategic priorities.
Critical Minerals Support Clean Energy and Advanced Technologies
Critical minerals such as copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt and rare earth elements are essential for clean energy technologies and electrification. They support the manufacturing of wind turbines, electricity transmission networks, electric vehicles and batteries. As demand for these materials increases, reliable access to critical minerals has become increasingly important for industrial development and the energy transition.
Policy Aims to Strengthen Domestic Supply Security
The proposed stockpiling policy and the planned processing parks represent key steps towards strengthening India’s critical minerals supply chain. Together, these initiatives aim to improve domestic processing capabilities, support value addition and ensure a more reliable supply of essential materials for industries that depend on them. articles.title: France's 2027 Finance Bill Could Trigger Over €5 Billion in Private Hydrogen Investment - energynews.pro
articles.summary: France's 2027 Finance Bill Could Trigger Over €5 Billion in Private Hydrogen Investment  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
France Hydrogène welcomes the presentation of the 2027 finance bill (PLF), which includes three measures the sector had been awaiting. They are a double-auction mechanism for synthetic aviation fuels (e-SAF), the entry into force of the Incentive to Reduce the Carbon Intensity of Fuels (IRICC) and the launch of the second tranche of the support mechanism for low-carbon hydrogen production (MSP), worth €1.2 billion. According to the association, these measures were among the priorities identified at the steering committee of the Hydrogen Strategy on July 22, aimed at helping French industrial projects reach final investment decisions. The topic comes amid a European context in which the expansion of hydrogen in the EU is expected to weigh little on most water resources.
A double-auction mechanism for e-SAF
According to France Hydrogène, France holds the largest portfolio of e-SAF projects in Europe and the second largest in the world, behind China. Demand for e-SAF is underpinned by the ReFuelEU Aviation regulation. The double-auction mechanism is meant to reconcile producers, who need commitments of 10 to 15 years to secure their investments, with consumers, who can hardly commit beyond 3 years. Elsewhere, demand for sustainable aviation fuels is driving other initiatives, such as India's effort to secure its used cooking oil supply to produce SAF.
The association says twelve French projects could be commissioned between 2030 and 2035. They would represent more than 800,000 tonnes of annual e-SAF production capacity and more than 14 billion euros in potential investment.
Electrolysis, jobs and guaranteed volumes
According to France Hydrogène, delivering these projects would mobilize 3.4 GW of electrolysis, equivalent to 40% of the target set by the National Hydrogen Strategy for 2035. It would create more than 3,600 permanent direct and indirect jobs to operate the sites. Nearly 27 TWh of decarbonized electricity would be turned into industrial added value within the country.
The mechanism planned by the government would guarantee up to 160,000 tonnes of e-SAF production per year. This volume corresponds to the 2% mandate set for 2032 by ReFuelEU Aviation. The association links it to two large projects, representing close to €3 billion in private investment.
The IRICC and the second MSP tranche
France Hydrogène welcomes the inclusion of the IRICC in the finance bill, which it expects to secure demand for renewable and low-carbon hydrogen in refining, maritime synthetic fuels and road mobility. The association estimates the incentive should trigger close to €2 billion in private investment in these sectors. That figure is a median value, which depends on the size of the hydrogen quota ultimately adopted.
Following the announcement of the first MSP winners this summer, the budget confirms the €1.2 billion envelope to fund the second tranche, launched in September. According to the association, the mechanism should lead to new final investment decisions in steelmaking, fertilizers and chemicals.
Nicolas Brahy, president of France Hydrogène, says the sector is "at a pivotal moment" and must resume major final investment decisions in 2027. He adds: "If these three measures are voted, French potential will finally be turned into industrial investment."

Natural gas provides reliable power that can complement intermittent renewable sources such as wind and solar. As electricity demand rises, utilities and industries are turning to gas for dependable supply.

Researchers at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands have found that long-term revenue guarantees are essential to making large-scale green hydrogen projects financially viable. The study modeled a 200 MW electrolyzer in the Rotterdam-Rijnmond industrial cluster, comparing wholesale electricity purchases, green power purchase agreements (PPAs), and a hybrid configuration combining dedicated renewable generation with PPA-backed electricity supply. The levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) was approximately €7.2/kg to €7.3/kg for the PPA and hybrid configurations, compared with €7.7/kg for wholesale electricity sourcing. However, all three configurations remained financially unviable without additional support. Monte Carlo simulations showed that a hydrogen contract for difference (CfD) covering 100% of production over 15 years could significantly improve project bankability by stabilizing revenues and reducing financing costs. Under this scenario, the renewable-integrated configuration had a 0% to 6% probability of negative net present value (NPV), compared with higher risks under shorter contracts or partial volume coverage. The researchers said policymakers should prioritize long-term revenue support, allow integrated renewable energy and hydrogen projects to compete alongside PPA-based developments, and coordinate supply-side incentives with measures to stimulate renewable hydrogen demand.

- Freeport-McMoRan stayed in view as copper demand tied to electrification and grid expansion drew fresh attention.
- Mining and metals names traded with a firm tone as the broader resources complex stayed active.
- The data-center and infrastructure buildout kept copper near the center of the materials conversation.
Freeport-McMoRan Inc. (NYSE:FCX) Basic Materials Freeport-McMoran Copper & Gold Inc (NYSE:FCX) 73.30 USD -0.390 0.529% Last Updated at: 2026-10-12T20:37:00Z opened the week in focus as copper stayed near the center of market conversation, with the metal's role in electrification, grid expansion, and the broad buildout of computing infrastructure drawing renewed attention. The company is one of the most widely watched names in the metals and mining category, a producer whose fortunes track closely with the direction of the red metal that underpins so much modern construction and manufacturing. A firm tone across the resources complex kept the spotlight on large miners whose output feeds into power lines, wiring, machinery, and the vast electrical systems that modern economies depend upon.
The company belongs to a cluster of mining and materials names that tend to move broadly in step with sentiment toward industrial metals, and it has become a familiar reference point whenever the copper theme moves to the front of market talk. Because copper sits at the heart of electric grids, buildings, vehicles, and increasingly the power-hungry data centers tied to artificial intelligence, the name attracts attention whenever demand narratives for the metal firm up. Its place within the large-company S&P 500 basket adds to the way the stock is followed during active periods for the broader materials group, keeping it woven into discussions about how the metals cycle is unfolding.
A Major Copper Producer In Focus
Freeport-McMoRan built its name as one of the largest producers of copper outside of state-controlled operators, with a footprint that spans the Americas and a landmark complex in Indonesia. That scale has made the company a recurring touchpoint in discussions about how the metal flows from the ground to the global economy. When copper sentiment firms, the stock frequently features in the conversation because the company sits so visibly at the junction of mining and the industrial demand that copper serves. The attention to start the week reflected that familiar pattern rather than any single isolated event.
The appeal of a large, diversified miner is that it offers broad exposure to the metal across several major operating regions rather than a single deposit. Over the decades the company has developed open-pit and underground mines, processing facilities, and the logistics needed to move concentrate and refined metal to market. This breadth keeps the name relevant whenever the theme of resource supply meets rising demand. It also helps explain why the stock tends to move with the broader metals tape rather than in isolation.
How The Business Operates
At its core the company earns by extracting copper ore, processing it, and delivering refined metal and concentrate to customers across many industries. Gold and molybdenum are produced alongside copper at several sites, giving the business a mix of metals that move with different drivers. This blended output means the company benefits from strength in the red metal while gaining added exposure to precious and specialty metals. The structure is often cited when describing why a diversified miner can weather swings in any single commodity.
Beyond the mines themselves, the company runs smelting and refining capacity, along with the transport and port facilities needed to reach global buyers. Its operations stretch from the Americas to a large mining district in Indonesia, where an extensive underground development has become a defining part of the asset base. That geographic spread turns the company into something closer to a global supplier of industrial metal rather than a single-site operator. The breadth of these operations keeps the name central to debates about how copper supply will meet the demands placed on it.
Copper And The Electrification Theme
Copper has carried a firm tone as the metal's central role in electrification moves from a long-range idea to an everyday reality across many economies. Electric vehicles, renewable power systems, and the expansion of transmission grids all lean heavily on the metal, which conducts electricity with few rivals at reasonable cost. For a producer of the red metal, that shift shows up as steady demand from sectors that were far smaller a generation ago. The momentum around these themes has kept the broader mining group in the market spotlight.
The practical story is straightforward, since building out cleaner power and modern transport requires enormous volumes of wiring, cabling, and electrical components. As grids expand and electrify, the pull on copper tends to strengthen alongside them. The company has leaned into messaging around the metal's indispensable place in this transition. This emphasis places the name squarely within the wider conversation about how the world will source the materials that electrification demands.
The Data-Center And Infrastructure Buildout
A newer strand of the copper story runs through the rapid construction of data centers tied to artificial intelligence and cloud computing. These facilities require vast quantities of electrical infrastructure, from power distribution to cooling systems, and copper features heavily throughout. As operators race to add computing capacity, the demands placed on power delivery have grown in step. That dynamic has drawn fresh attention to the metals that make such buildout possible.
The connection between computing growth and raw-material demand has become a defining feature of how the copper theme is now described. Expanding electrical capacity to serve new facilities pulls on the same metal that grids and vehicles already require. For a large producer, this adds another source of steady industrial pull to an already broad demand base. The intersection of digital growth and physical infrastructure keeps the name connected to one of the market's most watched themes.
The Broader Market Environment
The wider backdrop remains firm, with major US indices trading near record highs and resource names drawing attention as the metals complex stays active. Enthusiasm around artificial intelligence and advanced computing has spilled into the materials that support that growth, and copper sits squarely within that halo. Mining names benefit from being both cyclical industrial businesses and suppliers of the metals that modern construction requires. The general tone has therefore been supportive for names tied to the theme.
At the same time, the opening of a fresh earnings season has sharpened focus on how companies are actually performing rather than simply how themes are trending. Large firms across many sectors begin reporting early in the cycle, which puts broad sentiment under the microscope. Against that setting, miners are watched for signals about demand across construction, manufacturing, and power. The interplay between a firm index backdrop and a new reporting season keeps the group actively traded.
Shifts Across The Metals Landscape
The metals landscape continues to evolve as demand patterns shift toward the materials that power electrification and digital growth. Copper has moved from a largely construction-linked metal to one central to the energy transition, broadening the base of industries that depend on it. This widening demand has become a defining feature of the category and a frequent theme in how the space is described. It also reinforces why large producers draw attention whenever the metal moves back into the headlines.
Another notable shift is the growing attention to where new supply will come from, since major deposits take many years to develop. The gap between long project timelines and rising demand has become a recurring point in discussions about the metal. The company has invested across its asset base to keep output flowing as these themes play out. These developments keep the name connected to the broader direction of the metals cycle rather than a single slice of it.
Where The Company Sits
Within the mining landscape, the company is widely regarded as a core reference point for exposure to the red metal, given its scale and the quality of its asset base. Its standing among the largest copper producers gives it a distinctive place in the category. That positioning has been reinforced by a steady program of development across its major operating regions. The result is a name that tends to anchor discussions about how the world sources industrial metal.
The company also carries meaningful exposure to gold and specialty metals, widening the range of drivers that touch the business. This mix broadens the base while keeping copper firmly at the center of the story. Balancing a flagship metal with complementary output is a recurring theme in how the business is described. The breadth of its reach keeps the name relevant across several corners of the resources complex.
Within the broader market, the company is frequently grouped among Metal and Mining Stocks that attract attention when copper and the wider resources theme move to the front of the conversation.
Recent Operational Developments
Recent messaging from the company has centered on sustaining and expanding output across its key districts, with particular attention to its large underground development abroad. These efforts span ore sequencing, processing capacity, and the logistics needed to move metal to market. The emphasis reflects a broader push across the industry to keep supply flowing as demand narratives strengthen. For a producer at this scale, such operational steadiness carries clear weight in how the business is viewed.

articles.summary: Can Hudbay Turn Record Copper Prices Into Lasting Growth?  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Copper prices have climbed near record highs on tight global supply.
- Hudbay is advancing its Copper World project in Arizona while generating strong cash flow.
- The miner operates copper assets in Canada and Peru.
As copper prices push toward record territory, Hudbay Minerals Inc. (TSX:HBM) Basic Materials HudBay Minerals Inc (TSX:HBM) 37.24 CAD +1.150 3.187% Last Updated at: 2026-10-09T20:00:00Z is emerging as one of the Canadian miners most closely tied to the metals strength. The Toronto-based copper producer, with operations in Manitoba, British Columbia and Peru and a major development project in Arizona, is a constituent of the S&P/TSX Composite Index. Hudbay has been generating strong free cash flow while working to reduce the risks around its Copper World project, a key piece of its long-term growth plans. With supply tight and demand rising from electrification and data centres, the company sits at the heart of the copper story.
Coppers Remarkable Run
Copper prices surged in the third quarter, reaching record closing levels in September before experiencing volatility. Global inventories have fallen to unusually low levels, and stockpiling in the United States and China has tightened supply elsewhere.
Demand continues to grow from power infrastructure, electric vehicles and data centre construction, while new supply has been slow to come online. A strike at a major Chilean mine operated by another producer has added to supply concerns.
Equities Lagging the Metal
Industry commentary has noted that copper equities underperformed the metal itself during the third quarter. That gap has drawn attention to producers whose valuations may not yet fully reflect higher copper prices.
What Hudbay Operates
Hudbays portfolio includes copper and gold operations in Manitoba, the Copper Mountain mine in British Columbia and the Constancia mine in Peru. These assets produce copper along with gold, zinc and other metals.
The company has expanded its copper footprint through acquisitions, including Copper Mountain, and continues to invest in its existing operations.
Copper World in Arizona
Copper World is Hudbays major development project near Tucson, Arizona. The project is designed to become a significant domestic US copper source, an attractive feature given US efforts to secure supplies of critical minerals. Hudbay has been working to de-risk the project, including permitting and financing steps.
Strong Cash Generation
Higher copper and gold prices have supported strong free cash flow at Hudbay. That cash helps fund growth projects and strengthen the balance sheet without relying heavily on new financing.
For followers of Metal & Mining Stocks, Hudbays combination of current production, cash generation and a large development project offers a distinct profile among mid-sized copper producers.
The Policy Backdrop
US trade policy has influenced copper markets this year, including decisions on tariffs for refined copper. Reports last month that a US tariff plan had stalled triggered a sharp drop in copper and mining shares, showing how sensitive the sector is to policy news.
For Hudbay, a US-based copper project could benefit from policies supporting domestic supply, though the direction of trade policy remains uncertain.
Copper and the Energy Transition
Copper is essential for electrical wiring, power grids, electric vehicles and renewable energy systems. As countries invest in electrification and grid upgrades, demand for copper is expected to remain strong for years. Data centres supporting artificial intelligence add another layer of demand.
At the same time, new copper supply has been slow to emerge. Large mines take many years to permit and build, and many existing mines face declining grades. That gap between demand and supply underpins the strength in copper prices.
Gold as a Valuable By-Product
Many of Hudbays operations produce gold alongside copper. With gold prices also elevated this year, by-product revenue helps lower the effective cost of producing copper and supports overall profitability.
Disciplined Growth
Hudbay has emphasized balancing growth with financial discipline, using cash flow from existing operations to advance projects while maintaining a healthy balance sheet. That approach can reduce the need for dilutive financing as Copper World moves forward.
What Comes Next
Hudbay will report third-quarter results in the coming weeks, offering updates on production, costs, cash flow and progress at Copper World. The direction of copper prices and US trade policy will also shape the outlook.
With copper near record levels, Hudbay remains one of the most direct ways to follow the metals strength on the Canadian exchange.

articles.title: Piped through a Pennsylvania gas well as a nuisance for decades, 97 percent of the lithium in that oilfield water leaves as battery carbonate, and no mine was needed to produce it - Energies Media
articles.summary: Piped through a Pennsylvania gas well as a nuisance for decades, 97 percent of the lithium in that oilfield water leaves as battery carbonate, and no mine was needed to produce it  Energies Media
articles.full_text:
Every gas well in Pennsylvania’s Marcellus Shale brings something up that nobody ordered.
Millions of gallons of water, salty and laced with minerals, that the driller has to haul away.
For years, operators paid to dispose of it.
The plant sits in Montrose, a small borough in Susquehanna County in the wooded hill country of northeastern Pennsylvania that locals call the Endless Mountains.
Then a water recovery team discovered the nuisance carried dissolved lithium in concentrations high enough to matter.
A plant in Susquehanna County now converts that water into carbonate pure enough for an EV battery pack.
So what finally made that conversion possible, after years of treating the water as waste?
Three steps, one skid: how the conversion physically works
The core challenge with lithium dissolved in produced water is concentration. Oilfield brine may carry a few hundred parts per million of lithium alongside sodium, calcium, magnesium and a dozen other ions. Conventional evaporation ponds take months to bring that mixture anywhere near usable.
The process short circuits the wait with three linked stages running on a single compact unit. First, direct lithium extraction pulls lithium ions selectively out of the brine using a sorbent material, leaving the bulk of the salt solution behind. Because no evaporation pond is involved, the footprint fits inside a standard industrial skid rather than across an open desert basin.
Second, the lithium rich eluent goes through a concentration step that tightens the solution further. Third, a chemical conversion stage precipitates the lithium as carbonate, running continuously rather than in batches, which is why the output matches strict battery specifications.
A wellhead in the Endless Mountains, not a brine lake in the Atacama
The plant sits in Montrose, a small borough in Susquehanna County in the wooded hill country of northeastern Pennsylvania that locals call the Endless Mountains. It is about as far from the lithium triangle of South America as an energy facility can get and still serve a domestic supply chain.
The Marcellus Shale Formation beneath it is famous for natural gas, not lithium. Gas drillers there have been managing enormous volumes of produced water for more than a decade, building out disposal wells and water handling infrastructure that now serves a second purpose entirely.
The lithium extraction unit connects directly to those existing lines, which means no new wells and no new permits for mineral extraction were required to start the process. That infrastructure shortcut is part of what makes the economics work, since the water arrives at the unit because it always has.
What the live test actually measured
In testing at the Susquehanna County site, the facility demonstrated 97 percent lithium recovery from the produced water stream. It also produced lithium carbonate at a purity exceeding 99 percent, a specification that qualifies the output as battery grade material for electric vehicles and grid storage systems.
Both figures, the operator said, exceeded the targets the team had set going in. The commercial consequence followed quickly.
A multi year offtake agreement was signed to supply up to 5,000 metric tons annually of battery grade lithium carbonate to a US lithium ion battery manufacturer for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. The identity of the buyer was not disclosed, but the volume is meaningful, since the facility could ultimately supply half of domestic demand.
“We now have a fully operational lithium production asset in the U.S. that proves what EC² can deliver,” said the chief executive of the water recovery company behind the plant. “This isn’t a concept, it’s a live facility demonstrating that clean, domestic lithium production is both viable and scalable.”
Where the process still runs into limits
A 97 percent recovery rate at a single Pennsylvania well site does not automatically translate to identical results across every shale basin. Lithium concentration in produced water varies considerably from formation to formation, and even from well to well within the Marcellus itself.
So the economics of each new deployment depend on a water chemistry assessment before any equipment ships. The full commercial plant was targeted for commissioning by early 2026, and as of mid year the operator confirmed operations were on track.
Even so, scaling a continuous flow chemical process from a pilot skid to a facility supplying thousands of metric tons a year involves engineering steps that lab figures do not capture. Battery grade lithium carbonate is also only the starting material for cathode manufacturing, not the finished product. Work on other reactor byproducts shows that the value of a waste stream output depends heavily on where it sits in the downstream chain.
A new model for critical mineral supply, built on water nobody wanted
The most striking aspect of the Pennsylvania plant is what it does not require. There is no open pit, no tailings pond, no years of permitting for a new mine, and no dependence on a foreign processing facility.
According to the company’s release, the facility is fully owned and operated by the water recovery company, encompassing equipment, land, water and mineral rights, and all necessary permits. That is a vertically integrated model that bypasses many traditional project delays.
That matters because the United States has struggled to build a domestic critical mineral chain that keeps pace with battery manufacturing demand. Pulling the metal from water that drillers already handle turns an existing cost center into a supply asset.
The model also offers something that a grid battery fleet is beginning to demand at scale: a carbonate supply that does not hinge on a single overseas source. If the Marcellus site proves out at full production volume, the template could move to the Permian, the Bakken and any other basin where high volume water handling is already running. The oilfield’s oldest nuisance may yet become its most valuable output.

articles.title: Looking for iron ore on Google Earth, a man found an impact crater that had never been mapped by science - Earth.com
articles.summary: Looking for iron ore on Google Earth, a man found an impact crater that had never been mapped by science  Earth.com
articles.full_text:
A geologist found an undiscovered meteorite crater in Western Australia on Google Earth in 2007. Later drilling confirmed its iron meteorite origin.
In July 2007, geologist Arthur Hickman was scanning satellite images of Western Australia on Google Earth, looking for iron ore. Instead, he spotted a near-perfect circle in the rugged hills of the Pilbara region.
The feature turned out to be a meteorite impact crater about 850 feet (260 meters) wide. Despite decades of mining activity nearby, no one had recognized it before.
Today it is known as Hickman crater. It took years of fieldwork, drilling and lab analysis to prove that a falling iron meteorite carved it out.
A “flaw” on the screen
Hickman worked for the Geological Survey of Western Australia (GSWA). At the time, he was searching the imagery for channel iron deposits, a type of iron ore found in ancient riverbeds.
“I was looking from high up at about 20,000ft [6000m] and I saw this bubble-like shape, like a flaw on the image,” he told Australian Geographic.
The circle sits in the Ophthalmia Range, about 22 miles (36 kilometers) north-northwest of the mining town of Newman. Iron ore exploration and mining have been intense in the surrounding Hamersley Range since the 1960s.
GSWA had also mapped the area roughly two decades before Hickman’s discovery, without noticing the crater, according to a 2008 report in Universe Today.
Hickman sent screenshots and coordinates to colleagues at the Australian National University (ANU). Researcher Andrew Glikson named the crater after him, in recognition of the discovery and his 35 years of work on the geology of the Pilbara.
Studying the surface
The crater has a partly eroded rim that rises up to 98 feet (30 meters) above a flat, circular floor. Its shape matched that of other small impact craters.
In 2008, Glikson, Hickman and a colleague described the site in detail. They found shattered rock in the crater rim, cut by veins of the iron mineral goethite, and these features appeared only within the crater zone.
The team estimated that the original crater was about 260 feet (80 meters) deep. They suggested it was excavated by an object roughly 33 feet (10 meters) across, which threw debris up to about 980 feet (300 meters) north of the rim.
The crater looked young, likely dating to the Late Pleistocene, between 10,000 and 100,000 years ago.
But one key piece of evidence was missing. Surface samples showed no chemical traces of meteorite material, so the case for an impact still rested mostly on the crater’s shape and fractured rock.
Drilling into the crater floor
In late 2012, GSWA teamed up with the mining company Atlas Iron to drill a vertical hole in the center of the crater floor. The core reached a depth of 212 feet (64.7 meters).
According to GSWA geologist Peter Haines, it was the first scientific drilling of a simple impact crater of this size in Australia, as described in a Curtin University seminar.
The drill passed through nearly 165 feet (50 meters) of sediment that had filled the crater. Below that lay about 20 feet (6 meters) of impact breccia, a layer of crushed and partly melted rock, before the bit reached the original bedrock.
That breccia held the missing evidence. Nickel levels reached up to 2,381 parts per million, compared with less than 3 parts per million in the surrounding rock.
The layer was also enriched in iridium and other platinum group elements. These metals are scarce in typical Earth rocks but much more abundant in many meteorites.
Fingerprints of an iron meteorite
The chemistry pointed to an iron meteorite. Because the crater lacks some of the shock features seen at larger impact sites, researchers suggested the relatively small object was slowed significantly by the atmosphere before it hit.
In 2018, the first fresh metallic meteorite associated with the crater was reported. It was classified as an iron meteorite of the IAB group and named Hickman.
In 2025, researchers from Curtin University and GSWA presented new results at the annual meeting of the Meteoritical Society. They studied glass formed by the impact, which they described as extremely bubbly and similar to pumice.
Inside the glass, the team found tiny iron-nickel spherules and elevated levels of iron, nickel, cobalt and platinum group elements. One spherule, just 20 micrometers across, contained 33 percent nickel.
The researchers concluded that this material, together with the earlier drilling results, provides “unambiguous diagnostic evidence of a meteorite impact origin for Hickman crater.”
Craters still hiding in plain sight
Hickman crater shows how easily small impact sites can blend into the landscape. Erosion, vegetation and rough terrain can hide them even in well-explored regions.
Satellite images continue to reveal new candidates. In 2026, scientists reported a much larger crater in Quebec that was first spotted by an amateur astronomer on online satellite maps.
The Pilbara itself holds far older scars. Researchers have identified what is now considered Earth’s oldest known crater in the same region, and some scientists think such impacts may have created environments for early life.
Iron meteorites like the one that formed Hickman crater are also valuable to scientists because they preserve clues about how the solar system formed. Their metal content can reveal where their parent bodies took shape.
For Hickman, the find began with a routine search for iron ore. It ended with a crater named after him.
The original study was published in the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences.
