articles.title: China's Lithium Carbonate Futures Plunge Nearly 12%, Breaching 110,000 Yuan as Institutions Warn of 2027 Oversupply - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: China's Lithium Carbonate Futures Plunge Nearly 12%, Breaching 110,000 Yuan as Institutions Warn of 2027 Oversupply  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Lithium carbonate futures on China's Guangzhou Futures Exchange broke below the 110,000 yuan per ton level on October 12, capping an eight-week losing streak. The most-active LC2701 contract opened lower and extended losses throughout the session, closing down 11.79% at 104,740 yuan (approximately $15,700) per ton — the first sub-110,000 yuan close since late December last year. Compared with the mid-May stage high above 200,000 yuan per ton, current prices have nearly halved; since September alone, the cumulative decline has exceeded 37%.
The sharp futures selloff quickly spilled over into the equity market. Chinese A-share lithium miners fell broadly on the day: Youngy Co. (002192.SZ) and Shengxin Lithium (002240.SZ) both closed down nearly 7%, Tianqi Lithium (002466.SZ) slid more than 5%, and Ganfeng Lithium (002460.SZ) dropped nearly 4%. The lithium battery sector, which had been outperforming the broader market, also reversed course after an early-session rally.
Front-running funds and supply expectations converge
The current period is seasonally strong for lithium demand, and spot supply-demand conditions remain tight. Yet the futures market's pricing focus has clearly shifted toward next year's supply-demand expectations. Wang Meidan, an analyst at CITIC Futures, noted that this round of declines stems primarily from expectation revisions — the market is pessimistic about longer-term demand prospects, and some funds have positioned early with clear front-running signals, causing the board to price in a looser distant-month supply-demand balance.
Positioning data corroborates the fund-driven nature of the move. According to Wind data, as of the October 12 close, open interest in the most-active lithium carbonate futures contract stood at approximately 429,000 lots, up about 7,401 lots from the prior session — a 1.76% daily increase — reflecting rising open interest alongside falling prices. Peng Yuzhe, an analyst at Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), believes September's price action — down, then up, then down again — was driven largely by clustered fund trading. He does not rule out a concentrated liquidation of long positions in the near term, though prices could recover once sentiment is fully flushed out.
Marginal supply-side changes are also adding pressure. On October 8, 2026, the Yichun Municipal Ecology and Environment Bureau re-published the environmental impact assessment acceptance notice for the Jianxiawo lithium mine, restarting the approval process. As the world's largest single lepidolite lithium mine, the progress of its approval has reinforced expectations of incremental domestic supply in China. Funeng Futures noted that this development constitutes a marginal bearish factor for the board.
Institutions collectively slash lithium price forecasts
Several leading institutions have recently published reports expressing a more cautious medium-term outlook for the lithium market.
Goldman Sachs' global metals and mining research team, in a report released October 6, projected that the global lithium market will swing from a supply deficit of 404,000 tons in 2026 to a surplus of 444,000 tons in 2028. On price forecasts, Goldman expects China's average lithium carbonate spot price to fall to roughly 100,000 yuan (approximately $15,000) per ton in 2027, and further to 84,000 yuan (approximately $13,000) per ton in 2028 — a decline of about 42% from the projected 2026 average.
CITIC Securities has also turned more cautious. The Chinese brokerage expects the global lithium market to flip to a surplus of 38,000 tons in 2027, and has lowered its fourth-quarter 2026 lithium price range forecast to 100,000–150,000 yuan per ton. CITIC Securities attributed the price decline primarily to weak expectations suppressing strong fundamentals: overseas lithium mine and salt lake project output in the second quarter of 2026 showed growth both quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, and the acceleration of restarts and expansions across global lithium resource producers — combined with market concerns about slowing demand growth — has jointly weighed on lithium prices.
Notably, these two institutions' judgments from just a few months ago stand in stark contrast to their current views. In May of this year, CITIC Securities had projected that favorable supply-demand dynamics could push lithium prices to 250,000 yuan (approximately $37,000) per ton within two to three months. Goldman Sachs, in mid-June research notes, also believed the fourth quarter would be the tightest supply-demand period of the year, forecasting mainstream lithium carbonate prices around 200,000 yuan (approximately $30,000) per ton with peaks reaching 250,000 yuan. The market, however, did not follow the script — premium battery-grade lithium carbonate prices have already fallen below 120,000 yuan (approximately $18,000) per ton.
| Institution | Forecast Date | 2026 Supply-Demand | 2027 Supply-Demand | 2027 China Spot Average Forecast | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Goldman Sachs | Oct 2026 | Deficit of 404,000 tons | — | ~100,000 yuan/ton | 
| CITIC Securities | Oct 2026 | — | Surplus of 38,000 tons | Q4 range: 100,000–150,000 yuan/ton | 
| Goldman Sachs | Jun 2026 | Q4 tightening | — | Q4 ~200,000 yuan/ton | 
| CITIC Securities | May 2026 | Supply contraction | — | Up to 250,000 yuan/ton in 2–3 months | 
Note: Goldman Sachs projects a 2028 global lithium market surplus of 444,000 tons, with China's spot average falling to roughly 84,000 yuan per ton.
Spot destocking continues but cost pressure mounts
While the futures board is dominated by bearish expectations, destocking and production scheduling in the spot market continue to advance.
According to SMM statistics, as of October 8, China's total lithium carbonate inventory stood at 139,517 tons, down 9,260 tons from before the National Day holiday — a destocking pace of approximately 6.2%. Over a longer horizon, total inventory has been drawn down from roughly 203,000 tons in early June to 113,600 tons by end-September, a cumulative decline of about 44%, with the pace of destocking notably faster than in the second quarter.
On the demand side, Mysteel survey data shows lithium iron phosphate (LFP) orders remained solid after the holiday, with leading production lines running at high utilization. China's LFP output reached 603,200 tons in September, and is expected to climb further to 625,000 tons in October — a month-over-month increase of about 3.6% — with December production schedules approaching 650,000 tons, a new high for the year.
The breach below 110,000 yuan per ton means the supply chain is recalculating costs and inventory. For upstream lithium salt producers, this price level has touched the breakeven line for some high-cost capacity. Industry sources indicate that some enterprises producing lithium carbonate from purchased spodumene have costs around 140,000 yuan (approximately $21,000) per ton, and pressure is mounting simultaneously on multiple fronts: production cuts, maintenance shutdowns, hedging, and long-term contract renegotiations. If prices continue to fall, further production cuts at high-cost lines cannot be ruled out. The industry is undergoing a profound reshuffling, with high-cost capacity set to be cleared out at an accelerated pace.
Fourth-quarter focus: supply disruptions and destocking sustainability
On the outlook, the consensus among most analysts is for near-term weakness with volatility, and a medium-term focus on whether destocking can continue to build support. Peng Yuzhe believes that as destocking across the entire supply chain extends through year-end, the inventory-to-sales ratio will decline and the market will gradually return to fundamentals-based pricing.
On the supply side, lithium ore arrivals at Chinese ports are expected to rise in the fourth quarter. Overseas mine project output and shipments are generally in recovery, and with a significant increase in arrivals from Zimbabwe and Australia, incremental supply will be gradually released. Wei Chaoming, chief new-energy researcher at Founder CIFCO Futures, told Yicai that fourth-quarter lithium carbonate prices are likely to show a wide-range bottoming pattern: falling inventories, warrant outflows, and resilient spot prices provide some support, but concentrated arrivals of African ore and the difficulty of falsifying distant-month oversupply expectations will weigh on prices.
Mysteel's latest survey also points to a dual characteristic in the fourth quarter of 2026: "demand exceeding expectations, supply falling short." Downstream LFP and battery cell production schedules continue to be revised upward, with December likely to set a new annual high; meanwhile, slowing domestic output growth in China, declining Chilean exports, and cost inversion for purchased-ore producers are collectively constraining supply increments. Against the backdrop of sustained destocking, November's total inventory days could fall to around 15 days — an annual low — and with the buffer function of trader inventories weakened, price sensitivity to supply disruptions has risen significantly.
Key variables to watch going forward include: the actual enforcement of Zimbabwe's export restrictions and changes in arrival volumes, the pace of easing in Jiangxi lepidolite supply tightness, whether Chilean export volumes can rebound in the fourth quarter, and the actual realization of downstream LFP production schedules and inventory-day trends. Any one of these factors exceeding expectations could become the key variable that breaks the current supply-demand balance.
Wei Chaoming also cautioned that attention should be paid to multiple factors including supply disruption repricing, policy changes, supply disruptions in resource-rich countries, the acceleration of sodium-ion battery substitution, and macro and currency dynamics. articles.title: Copper at a Record, but the Tariff Trade Is Fading for COMEX_MINI:MHG1! by mintdotfinance - TradingView
articles.summary: Copper at a Record, but the Tariff Trade Is Fading for COMEX_MINI:MHG1! by mintdotfinance  TradingView
articles.full_text:
On 9 September 2026, front-month LME copper set an all-time high of $14,940 per tonne. COMEX Copper Futures followed with its own record of $6.9285 per lb on 22 September. Both have since pulled back. 
The force behind the rally was not a shortage. Traders were pricing in an expected US tariff on imported refined copper. The logic was straightforward: copper already inside the US would be worth more than copper sitting elsewhere if a tariff came, so metal was shipped to COMEX warehouses ahead of it. The gap between the two, the tariff premium, opened to several hundred dollars per tonne before collapsing.
Two events drove that collapse. On 10 September, the White House signalled that refined copper tariffs remained unresolved. COMEX fell sharply intraday. On 28 September, the White House’s deadline for a decision passed without an announcement. The market read both as the tariff not coming, at least for now.
Copper still trades near record levels. But the clearest driver of the rally has weakened. That is the tension this paper examines. 
The Inventory Shift
US copper stocks more than doubled in a year. COMEX warehouses held around 711,600 metric tonnes, as of 7 October, still near record highs. LME stocks drained to multi-year lows by August and have only partially recovered. SHFE copper inventories stand at 58,744 tonnes as of this writing, down by nearly 86% from its March peak. The world did not produce more copper. Tariff anticipation moved it from London and Shanghai into US warehouses. 
The tightness in London looked alarming. The LME cash price rose sharply above the three-month futures price, a condition called backwardation that typically signals buyers are scrambling for metal right now. However, the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) was reporting a global refined surplus the entire time. The backwardation was the mirror image of the COMEX build, not a sign that the world was running short. 
The flow has now stopped. New shipments into the US stopped making economic sense once the tariff premium narrowed. The copper already in US warehouses is unlikely to move back quickly given the cost of re-exporting it.
What the Fundamentals Show 
China accounts for more than half of global copper consumption. Demand has grown this year on grid investment, electric vehicles, and renewables, but not at a pace that explains record prices. China’s Golden Week holiday runs through the first week of October, typically followed by a burst of factory restocking. When trading resumed, the premium buyers paid to import physical copper rose, but actual deals were thin.
On the supply side, Chile is adding risk. A strike began 7 October at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine, which produced 240,400 metric tonnes last year. Two unions representing 709 workers walked out after mediation failed over a pay dispute dating to 2020. Antofagasta expects no production impact; whereas the unions warn of supply effects by November. As copper prices have risen, so have tensions between miners and management across Chile, making disruptions harder to contain.
The International Copper Study Group projects a refined surplus of around 96,000 tonnes in 2026, widening to 377,000 tonnes in 2027. Its figures exclude unreported Chinese stocks, leaving some uncertainty. The headline balance does not support a shortage narrative. Sustained inventory draws paired with spot premiums backed by actual end-user orders would change that picture. That evidence does not yet exist.
The Macro Headwind 
The Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00% on 16 September, the first hike since 2023. The hike sent the dollar higher, a direct headwind for copper. US Treasury yields are at multi-decade highs, keeping that pressure in place. 
Through August, gold and silver rallied while copper moved sideways. Gold and silver then fell sharply from their August highs, and fell further after the Fed’s rate hike. Copper rose after the hike and has held up. 
Gold and silver fell as expectations of Fed hikes rose. The war pushed oil and inflation higher, which lifted real yields (the return on bonds after inflation) and the dollar, and neither metal pays a yield. We explain this in detail in a previous paper. Copper took the dollar hit too, but tight supply outside the US, covered above, limited the decline. 
If the dollar and real yields stay elevated, copper faces growing downside pressure even as physical supply outside the US continues to tighten. 
Historical Trade Setup
8 October 2025: Teck cuts copper guidance
Early October 2025 offers a useful historical analogue for today. Chinese demand was uncertain after the Golden Week holiday and the dollar was firm, but mine disruptions kept supply concerns alive. Teck cut its 2025 copper guidance on 8 October, and the trade enters at the 9 October open.
On 10 October, copper fell as much as 5% after President Trump threatened additional tariffs on Chinese imports, and the position moved below its entry price. It recovered from 13 October as trade fears eased and mine disruptions kept supply tight. By 29 October, hopes for a US-China trade framework and the Fed’s rate cut expectations supported a bullish view, though weak Chinese buying capped the upside. The Fed was easing then and is tightening now, so this illustrates a comparable setup, not a forecast.

Entry: 5.1350 USD/lb, open, 9 October 2025
Exit: 5.3340 USD/lb, close, 29 October 2025
Move: 5.3340 − 5.1350 = 0.1990 USD/lb → 3.88%

articles.title: U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve Hits Lowest Level Since 1982 Amid Ongoing Oil Crisis - SSBCrack
articles.summary: U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve Hits Lowest Level Since 1982 Amid Ongoing Oil Crisis  SSBCrack
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has fallen to a critical low of 283 million barrels of oil as of the end of September, marking the lowest level since October 1982. This has raised concerns among analysts and commentators who warn that the current inventory presents challenges for both immediate energy security and future economic stability. Notably, the rapid depletion of the reserve stems from significant drawdowns, particularly following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which prompted the Biden administration to release 180 million barrels.
Historically, the SPR was established in 1975 in response to the Arab oil embargo, designed to protect the nation from oil supply shocks. Over the years, it peaked at 726.6 million barrels in 2009, but has seen a steady decline since then. The Biden administration’s drawdown has been described as the largest in the reserve’s history, which has left the SPR in a precarious position.
While oil can be removed from the SPR quickly, putting it back is a far slower and costlier process. Recent efforts to refill the reserve have seen the Department of Energy (DOE) facilitating exchanges, wherein companies essentially borrow oil and are required to return more than they took—often at steep premiums. These exchanges, though termed as loans, put additional pressure on companies to locate barrels in a tight market upon repayment.
As the SPR continues to dwindle, questions arise regarding where the bottom truly lies. The DOE claims that the caverns remain structurally sound, asserting that a minimum of 70 million barrels is sufficient for operational purposes. However, energy experts suggest that the effective operational threshold could be closer to 250 million barrels, and a significant portion of industry executives indicated a belief that inventories dropping below 150 million barrels would be alarming.
The SPR’s design allows for withdrawals at approximately six times the rate at which it can be filled. Under current conditions, filling it back up will be an arduous process, requiring years to restore even to a suboptimal level. Structural integrity concerns have emerged, especially with several caverns nearing their limits. Technical issues, such as well failures, threaten to complicate the situation further.
Financially, the DOE’s exchanges do not solve the long-term funding dilemma required to replenish the SPR. Estimates suggest it will cost around $20 billion to restore the reserve to its effective peak capacity, an expense that has yet to be allocated in the federal budget. Current plans to refill the SPR may not be sustainable without new financial provisions.
Further complicating the landscape, the SPR also serves as a critical buffer in the event of not just geopolitical crises but domestic disruptions, such as natural disasters. With the ongoing threat of hurricanes impacting oil infrastructure, a thin reserve could jeopardize response capabilities in future emergencies.
The implications of current strategies extend beyond just the reserve’s operational capacity. Oil market dynamics indicate that the demand generated by replenishing the SPR could drive prices higher, potentially raising costs for consumers. As the geopolitical climate remains volatile, the challenges associated with the SPR underscore the delicate balance of energy policy and economic stability.
As the situation evolves, many are left pondering the extent to which the SPR can serve its intended purpose without further compounding existing challenges in both local and global oil markets. The path ahead is fraught with uncertainty, dependent on both market conditions and policy decisions that will shape energy security for years to come.

articles.title: Qatar’s LNG exports may fall to 0.6 million tonnes in October — Cyprus Mail - UA.NEWS
articles.summary: Qatar’s LNG exports may fall to 0.6 million tonnes in October — Cyprus Mail  UA.NEWS

In Qatar, exports of liquefied natural gas remain significantly restricted despite a partial recovery in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. According to Cyprus Mail, analytics company Kpler estimates that Qatari LNG shipments could decline to 0.6 million tonnes in October, down from 1.6 million tonnes in September. The publication notes that the decline is likely linked to an increase in attacks on vessels.
September’s figure was the highest since the start of the conflict, but it amounted to less than a quarter of the pre-war average level, according to Kpler. About one-third of the volume exported in September went to Kuwait, meaning it remained within the Persian Gulf. The remaining cargoes were sent to China, India and other Asian countries.
Oil shipments are recovering faster
Shipments of Middle Eastern oil through the Strait of Hormuz rose in September to around 80% of the pre-war level, reaching 16 million barrels per day, according to Kpler data. This enabled Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Iraq to significantly increase production.
At the same time, LNG transportation is recovering much more slowly. Last month, QatarEnergy extended force majeure notices, indicating an inability to deliver cargoes to many customers in Asia and Europe. As Cyprus Mail notes, there are far fewer LNG tankers than oil tankers, and they are more expensive to operate, so carriers are reluctant to pass through the strait when there is a risk of attacks or a prolonged blockade.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Constraints on production
Qatar is the world’s second-largest LNG producer after the United States and has capacity of nearly 80 million tonnes per year, or around one-fifth of global capacity. After hostilities began, the country was forced to shut down a significant part of the Ras Laffan complex. Iranian missile strikes, according to the publication, also disabled around 17% of export capacity.
To increase exports, Qatar needs to raise production at the North Field, which it shares with Iran. Condensate is produced alongside gas and requires separation and export. If it cannot be exported reliably, storage facilities may fill up quickly, limiting gas production. Qatar also has limited capacity to store LNG on land and on vessels.
The country is simultaneously implementing a programme to expand capacity to 142 million tonnes of LNG per year by 2030. However, the prospects for this project depend on stable and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: How the Green Hydrogen Summit Day Unfolds? - Business Viewpoint Magazine
articles.summary: How the Green Hydrogen Summit Day Unfolds?  Business Viewpoint Magazine
articles.full_text:
Boardrooms across Delhi are talking about a new kind of power. Investors ask about production costs. Manufacturers ask about supply. Policymakers ask about exports. At the centre of these conversations is a fuel once confined to research labs, now tied to factories, ports, and trade routes.
The 2nd Bharat Green Hydrogen Summit 2026, hosted by FICCI in New Delhi, gathers these voices under one roof, built around positioning India as a global energy hub. This piece walks through what happens at the summit and why industry watchers should take note.
The summit at a glance
- Event: 2nd Bharat Green Hydrogen Summit 2026
- Date: 23 July 2026
- Venue: FICCI Federation House, New Delhi
- Organiser: Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry (FICCI)
- Theme: “Positioning India as a Global Hydrogen Hub”
FICCI describes the summit as a meeting point for policymakers, government agencies, public sector units, industry leaders, financial institutions, technology providers, startups and academia.
The theme reflects the wider scope of the national mission.
It covers production, domestic consumption and export opportunities, along with the technology, infrastructure, financing and skilled talent needed to support them. Together, these priorities shape how India approaches clean energy manufacturing and trade at scale.
How the green hydrogen summit day unfold?
A single day at the summit moves through several stages, each building naturally on the one before it.
- Morning: Opening remarks and high-level policy perspectives on India’s hydrogen mission.
- Mid-morning: Government and industry hold talks on regulation, incentives, and timelines.
- Midday: Panels cover policy, investment, cost, infrastructure, technology, and global trends, FICCI’s five thematic areas.
- Afternoon: Talks turn to financing and domestic manufacturing of electrolysers and equipment.
- Throughout: Networking and knowledge exchange link Indian and international participants.
Similar events across India follow this same pattern, pulling policymakers, industry leaders, financiers, researchers and global stakeholders under one roof.
The big conversations: policy, cost and demand
Three questions dominate discussions at the summit, and each points to a different piece of the puzzle facing India’s clean-energy ambitions.
Can policy make projects easier to build?
Speakers are expected to raise regulatory clarity, certification standards, procurement rules, and firmer policy backing as conditions that could make projects easier to implement across states.
Can production become commercially viable?
The cost of renewable electricity, electrolyser economics and project financing all shape whether output can compete with existing fuels on price and reach commercial viability.
Who will buy it?
Without buyers, supply means little. Long-term offtake agreements and steady industrial demand in ammonia, steel, mobility and shipping will decide whether projects reach real scale.
The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy notes that the national programme covers demand creation, competitive procurement, certification, financial incentives, pilot projects, infrastructure and dedicated Green Hydrogen hubs, tying these questions to an already active policy framework.
Technology, manufacturing and infrastructure
Turning policy into working infrastructure is the real challenge. Panels at the summit are expected to examine what must exist on the ground:
- Electrolyser manufacturing, seen as central to reducing import dependence
- Reliable renewable power supply to run production at scale
- Water availability and resource planning for electrolysis
- Storage systems built for a highly reactive fuel
- Pipelines, tankers and distribution networks connecting producers to industrial users
- Dedicated hydrogen hubs clustering production, storage and consumption
- Domestic R&D aimed at improving efficiency and cutting costs
The Green Hydrogen Mission backs many of these pieces directly, with incentives for electrolyser manufacturing, production-linked support, hydrogen hubs and public-private research. These technical foundations are expected to shape the summit’s infrastructure and manufacturing sessions closely, underlining how much groundwork remains before wide deployment.
Investment, exports and India’s global opportunity
The commercial conversation is where the event turns practical, moving past technology and policy into hard questions of money and markets.
The business case: what’s on the table
| Area | What’s at Stake | 
| Financing | Large projects need capital, but lenders still see the sector as untested; speakers will look at bankable models built on clear demand signals | 
| Export infrastructure | Ports, pipelines and storage terminals must be ready before shipments can begin | 
| Global standards | International certification and buyer requirements will decide which projects qualify for overseas contracts | 
| Partnerships | Cross-border collaboration can bring funding, technology and offtake agreements together | 
| Derivatives | Green ammonia is expected to see rising demand as an early export product | 
For Indian manufacturers and project developers, these discussions point toward a genuine opening in global supply chains.
Who should pay attention to the event?
The Green Hydrogen Summit brings together several groups, each with a different reason to attend.
- Policymakers and government bodies: direct policy insight and regulatory updates
- Energy companies and PSUs: commercial connections and project leads
- Renewable energy developers: market knowledge and partnership options
- Hydrogen producers: cost benchmarks and buyer conversations
- Electrolyser and equipment manufacturers: technology exposure and demand signals
- Banks and investors: financing conversations and deal flow
- Technology companies and startups: visibility among industry decision-makers
- Research institutions and universities: access to applied, real-world use cases
- Potential hydrogen buyers: supplier contacts and pricing clarity
- International partners: entry points into India’s hydrogen mission
For most attendees, this works as one meeting point covering policy, finance, and technology together, saving the separate outreach each conversation would otherwise need.
Why this summit matters?
The Bharat Summit brings together policy, industry, and finance to answer one question: how does India turn its hydrogen ambitions into a working market?
1. Execution. It connects policy ambition with real business execution.
2. Collaboration. It brings producers, users, and infrastructure players into one room.
3. Finance. It gives companies a venue to work through financing and offtake questions.
4. Manufacturing. It puts domestic technology development on the table.
5. Global Reach. It links India’s hydrogen plans to buyers and partners abroad.
Together, these points show why the summit sits at the centre of India’s clean energy calendar. The Green Hydrogen Mission set out to build capacity; gatherings like this decide how that capacity gets used.
MNRE’s stated goal remains a country positioned as a global hub for producing, using, and exporting hydrogen and its derivatives.
Closing: what readers should take away
One Question to Watch
The Bharat Summit matters less for its speeches and more for the practical work behind them: pricing demand, weighing costs, planning infrastructure, testing technology, structuring investment, and building ties with buyers abroad. These conversations, not slogans, will decide how far India’s Green Hydrogen plans travel. That leaves one question worth watching: can the country turn its hydrogen ambitions into commercially viable projects at scale?

articles.title: Why Qatar’s LNG Exports May Take Years to Recover From the Iran War - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Why Qatar’s LNG Exports May Take Years to Recover From the Iran War  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
The recovery of Middle Eastern oil exports has done little to ease the disruption facing the global liquefied natural gas (LNG) market, as Qatar struggles to restore shipments amid continuing security risks in the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar, the world’s second-largest LNG producer after the United States, accounts for roughly one-fifth of global export capacity, with annual capacity of nearly 80 million metric tons. The US-Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted its energy industry, forcing shutdowns at its main LNG complex in Ras Laffan and exposing the vulnerability of Gulf energy exports to prolonged conflict.
Iranian missile attacks have also damaged infrastructure responsible for around 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. The resulting losses could cost the country tens of billions of dollars in annual revenue, while repairs may take years to complete.
The economic consequences are severe. The International Monetary Fund forecasts Qatar’s gross domestic product will contract by 8.6% in 2026, reversing pre-war expectations for growth of 6.1%.
Disruptions to Qatari LNG supplies, alongside reduced exports from the United Arab Emirates, have tightened global gas markets. A sharp increase in US LNG exports has provided some relief, with shipments rising by around 14% in 2026 from a year earlier to 123 million tons. However, the additional supply has not fully offset the losses from the Gulf.
Asia and Europe have been particularly exposed because of their reliance on imported LNG and limited alternatives for replacing disrupted shipments. LNG prices in both regions reached their highest levels since early 2023 in late September, nearly tripling from pre-war levels.
Even if the Strait of Hormuz reopens, Qatar’s recovery is unlikely to be immediate. The country’s tightly integrated production and export system faces logistical constraints that make LNG far more difficult to restore than crude oil shipments.
Why Oil Exports Are Recovering Faster Than LNG
The outlook for Middle Eastern crude exports has improved in recent weeks, as producers have increasingly resumed shipments through the Strait of Hormuz despite continuing security threats.
According to data analytics firm Kpler, crude shipments through the waterway rose in September to around 16 million barrels per day, approximately 80% of pre-war levels. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait and Iraq have also increased domestic production as export conditions have improved.
LNG shipments, however, have remained severely constrained.
Qatar’s LNG exports reached 1.6 million tons in September, their highest level since the conflict began but still less than one-quarter of their pre-war average, according to Kpler. Around one-third of those shipments went to Kuwait, remaining within the Gulf, while the rest went to China, India and other Asian destinations.
The recovery could prove temporary. Qatar’s LNG exports in October are projected to fall to around 0.6 million tons, according to Kpler, amid renewed attacks on shipping. QatarEnergy has also extended force majeure notices, indicating that it remains unable to fulfil certain contractual deliveries to customers in Asia and Europe.
The difference between oil and gas exports reflects how their supply chains operate. Crude oil can be stored in large quantities, transported through alternative routes in some cases and supplied using a comparatively flexible shipping network. LNG requires specialised production facilities, temperature-controlled storage and dedicated carriers.
As a result, occasional safe passage through Hormuz is insufficient to restore Qatar’s export industry. Producers and shipping companies need confidence that vessels can repeatedly transit the waterway without facing unacceptable risks.
Qatar’s LNG Infrastructure Faces Complex Constraints
Qatar’s export system depends on 14 LNG production units, known as trains, supplied by natural gas extracted from the offshore North Field, the world’s largest natural gas reservoir, which Qatar shares with Iran.
Production has remained at minimal levels since the war began, supporting domestic demand and limited exports. Restoring output requires more than reopening the export terminal: gas production, processing, storage and shipping must all function together.
One complication is condensate, a light liquid hydrocarbon extracted alongside natural gas. Qatar must separate and export these liquids as part of its upstream production system. If condensate shipments cannot leave the Gulf reliably, storage constraints could eventually force producers to reduce gas output.
LNG storage presents another challenge. Qatar has limited capacity to hold large volumes of additional production onshore or aboard vessels while waiting for export routes to become available. Prolonged shipping delays can therefore disrupt operations even when global demand remains strong.
The availability of specialised LNG carriers is an additional constraint. Unlike crude oil tankers, LNG vessels operate within a more specialised shipping market, where capacity is less interchangeable and freight costs can be considerably higher. Shipowners may be reluctant to send expensive vessels through Hormuz if they risk being trapped inside the Gulf or damaged by attacks.
These constraints mean that a sustained recovery depends on reliable maritime access, functioning production infrastructure and a shipping industry willing to resume regular operations.
Qatar’s Expansion Plans Face a Security Test
The disruption comes at a critical point for Qatar, which is undertaking a major expansion of its LNG industry. The country plans to increase annual production capacity from nearly 80 million tons to 142 million tons by 2030, potentially raising its share of global LNG capacity to roughly one-quarter.
The expansion is intended to strengthen Qatar’s position in a market where demand for gas remains important to energy security, industrial production and electricity generation.
But additional production capacity offers limited economic value if exporters cannot reliably reach international customers. Continued insecurity in Hormuz could delay the commercial benefits of new facilities, complicate long-term supply contracts and encourage importers to diversify their energy sources.
The consequences extend beyond Qatar. Asian economies that rely heavily on Gulf LNG could face higher import costs and greater competition for alternative supplies. European buyers could also remain exposed to price volatility as they compete with Asian importers for cargoes from the United States and other producers.
For Qatar, the central challenge is therefore not simply restarting production but restoring confidence in the entire export chain.
A Lasting Recovery Depends on a Durable Regional Settlement
The future of Qatar’s LNG industry is increasingly tied to the security arrangements governing the Strait of Hormuz. A temporary reduction in hostilities or the passage of individual tankers may offer limited relief, but neither guarantees the predictable shipping conditions required for sustained exports.
A durable settlement involving Iran, the United States and regional powers would help reduce the risk of further attacks and give energy companies greater confidence to resume regular operations. Even then, damage to production facilities and disruptions to logistics could delay a return to pre-war supply levels.
The crisis also exposes a broader vulnerability in global energy markets: large investments in production capacity cannot guarantee energy security when exports depend on a single strategic maritime corridor.
Until Qatar can produce LNG at scale and ship it through Hormuz with confidence, the global gas market is likely to remain under pressure, and the country’s ambitious expansion programme will face an increasingly uncertain path.

articles.title: Is a Copper Rally Lifting Southern Copper (NYSE:SCCO)? - Kalkine Media

articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Copper prices have surged toward record levels on tight supply and firm demand.
- Southern Copper ranks among the lowest-cost copper producers in the world.
- Its large reserve base ties it closely to the electrification demand story.
With operations anchored in Peru and Mexico and a reserve base among the largest in the industry, the company tends to rise and fall with the red metal, and the recent strength has placed it near the front of the rally. Copper has firmed as supply disruptions have collided with steady demand tied to electrification, grids and construction. For a producer whose fortunes are so tightly bound to a sole metal, that strength feeds almost directly through to sentiment around the stock, and the market has responded in kind.
Sector Background
Copper is often described as the metal that wires the modern world. It carries electricity through homes, factories and grids, and sits at the heart of electrified transport, renewable power and the data centers springing up to feed computing demand. That breadth makes copper a widely watched gauge of industrial health. Because new copper supply is slow and costly to bring online, the market can tighten quickly when demand runs ahead of what miners can deliver. That dynamic has been a defining feature of the recent rally, and it places established producers with large reserves in a favorable spot.
Company Operations
Southern Copper runs integrated mining, smelting and refining operations, with its core assets located in Peru and Mexico. Glenfarne Group, LLC welcomed President Donald J. Trump's announcement of a $50 billion-plus South Korean investment in Alaska LNG, marking a major financing milestone that advances the project toward a final investment decision (FID) and construction.
Glenfarne CEO and Founder Brendan Duval joined Trump in the Oval Office for the announcement. Commercial progress and project scale
The announcement builds on 18 months of work by Glenfarne to advance Alaska LNG. "We came to Alaska to build this project, and every decision we make starts with what will move us closer to delivering affordable, reliable gas and long-term economic benefits for Alaskans," said Duval. We are ready to deliver on the opportunity Alaska LNG represents for Alaska and the United States."

This investment gives us the scale of capital needed, and we will keep working to make sure Alaska captures the jobs, economic opportunity and long-term value this project can create."

Glenfarne Group is a privately held global developer, owner, and operator of energy infrastructure assets. Through its subsidiaries, Glenfarne owns and operates 60 energy assets across three core businesses: Global LNG Solutions, Grid Stability, and Renewables.
